$comment: THE AZURE IDENTITY POLICY. One registry, two enforcers.
Every Azure resource this platform reaches is listed here exactly once, together with whether
managed identity is required for it and — where it is not — the named reason. Both deployables
enforce this file: ragcore/tests/security/test_azure_identity.py and
dotnet/tests/Synthia.ArchitectureTests/AzureIdentityTests.cs. A third test on each side asserts
that the two enforcers cover the same resources, so a resource cannot be quietly dropped from
one platform while passing on the other.
WHY A SHARED FILE RATHER THAN A CONSTANT IN EACH LANGUAGE: two lists drift, and the drift is
invisible until the day the weaker of the two is the one that mattered. A rule that is easier
to satisfy on one stack than the other is a rule that decides where the insecure code gets
written.
TO ADD AN EXEMPTION you edit this file, name the provider limitation, and give it an owner and a
review date. That is deliberately more friction than adding a connection string, because the
exemption is the thing that needs review, not the credential.

rule.statement: Azure SDK clients authenticate as a managed identity in deployed environments. Application-owned Azure credentials — client secrets, shared access keys, SAS tokens, account keys, passwords — are rejected except where a provider explicitly does not support managed identity, and every such exception is named below.
rule.localDevelopment: DefaultAzureCredential resolves a developer identity locally through the same code path, so there is no separate local branch to get wrong. A credential type that only works on a laptop is still a violation: the rule is about what the code can express, not about where it happens to run.

credentialChain.$comment: One credential instance per process, shared by every client. A client that constructs its own is how a second, weaker auth path appears next to the first.

resources.name: PostgreSQL Flexible Server
resources.notes: Entra authentication is supported. The access token is presented in the password position, which is exactly why a literal password in a DSN is indistinguishable from correct usage at a glance — and why the DSN rule below is a separate assertion rather than folded into the credential rule.

resources.name: Azure Service Bus
resources.notes: Namespace is a fully qualified name, never a credential-bearing connection string.

resources.name: Azure SignalR
resources.notes: The data-plane REST client uses an Entra token for scope https://signalr.azure.com/.default.

resources.name: Azure Key Vault
resources.notes: Key Vault is the sole source of secret material, so a secret used to reach Key Vault would defeat the entire arrangement. There is no configuration under which this exemption could be granted.

resources.name: Azure AI Search
resources.notes: Both admin and query keys are application-owned credentials and are rejected.

resources.name: Azure AI Foundry / model gateway dependencies
resources.notes: Reached only through the AI Gateway, which is a policy function rather than an identity boundary — so the identity presented to it, and the identity it presents onward, are both managed identities. An API key here would also bypass per-organisation metering, because the key is not tied to a caller.

resources.name: Application Insights / Azure Monitor
resources.notes: Entra-authenticated ingestion is supported and is what this platform uses. The Application Insights connection string is configuration rather than a credential — it carries an ingestion endpoint and an instrumentation key, not a secret — but it is still resolved by reference so that no environment-specific value is committed.

resources.name: Redis
resources.condition: Azure Cache for Redis and Azure Managed Redis support Entra ID authentication on the tiers and configurations this platform selects. Managed identity is REQUIRED wherever the selected configuration supports it.
resources.notes: Listed as conditional rather than required because the support genuinely depends on the deployed tier — not because a password is an acceptable default. If a configuration is selected that does not support Entra authentication, that is an exemption and belongs in the list below with a named owner. Redis is transient-only in this platform, which lowers the blast radius of a compromise but does not change the rule.

$comment: NAMED EXEMPTIONS. Empty, and that is the intended state.
An entry here means a provider genuinely does not support managed identity — not that
managed identity was inconvenient to wire up. Each entry requires: the resource id, the
provider limitation in one sentence, the credential type used instead, where it is stored
(which must be Key Vault), an owner, and a review date.
Third-party systems reached through MCP — ServiceNow, OneLogin, Duo — are NOT listed here.
They are not Azure resources, and their credentials are already governed by
tenant_entitlement.credential_reference, which holds a Key Vault reference and never a value.

exemptions.name: Azure Container Apps ingress — gateway provenance
exemptions.providerLimitation: Container Apps built-in authentication (Easy Auth), which is what would validate a managed-identity token at the ingress layer, is documented only for external ingress-enabled apps. These backends are internal-only by design, and validating the token in application code instead is prohibited by constitution Principle I — services MUST NOT parse an access token. Mutual TLS is the mechanism Container Apps documents for this case, with no such restriction.
exemptions.credentialType: client certificate (mutual TLS), presented by APIM and validated by ingress
$comment: WHAT IS ACTUALLY EXEMPTED HERE IS NARROW, and worth stating precisely so the review has
something to review. No component holds a standing secret: the private key is in Key Vault,
APIM reads it as a managed identity, and the backends hold only a public SHA-256 hash. The
exemption is therefore not 'a credential lives outside the vault' — it is that this
credential has a LIFECYCLE and an EXPIRY, which a managed identity would not.
That residual is managed rather than accepted: rotation is a sequenced release
(docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md) and expiry is alerted 45 days ahead
(expiryMonitoring in build/policy/edge-trust.json). Both are asserted by the edge trust
tests on each stack, so removing either one fails the build.
REVISIT THIS WHEN Container Apps documents Easy Auth for internal ingress. At that point
APIM's authentication-managed-identity policy plus an ingress-injected principal check
would remove the certificate entirely, and this entry with it. The backend middleware is
already shaped for that swap: it compares a platform-injected header against an allow-list,
and only the header name and the allow-list contents would change.
ON THE REVIEW DATE. It is a reminder, not a deadline, and the distinction is worth stating
because every other date in this file could be read as one. This exemption's exit condition
is EXTERNAL - it ends when Microsoft documents that feature - so no date predicts it. The
date answers 'when will somebody next look at this', and twelve months is a placeholder
chosen in the absence of a better anchor.
THERE IS A BETTER ANCHOR ONCE THE CERTIFICATE EXISTS: re-set this to roughly a month before
its first expiry. Whoever performs that rotation is already reading
docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md and already has the context loaded, so the
review costs them almost nothing - whereas a date landing in an arbitrary week is an
interruption, and an interruption is what gets deferred.

forbiddenEverywhere.$comment: Matched against production source and committed configuration on both stacks, irrespective of resource. These are the shapes an application-owned Azure credential actually takes.
